description: We are a team of two BTech students from CSE (AI/ML) and Data Science. We are interested in AI/ML, software development, and solving real-world problems. We are looking for enthusiastic teammates with skills in web/app development, UI/UX, data visualization, cloud technologies, or other relevant areas. Let’s collaborate, learn, and build an innovative solution for the NASA Space Apps Challenge!
summary:
ASTRA Junior is a browser-based astronaut mission trainer designed for learners ages 7–12. We developed ten interactive missions that teach systems thinking through astronaut-style decisions involving oxygen, water, power, food, materials, safety, and crew health.

The project addresses the challenge of building a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer by turning space science into an active learning experience rather than a collection of facts. Learners prepare equipment, choose between competing options, explain their reasoning, and observe the immediate and delayed consequences of their decisions. The game also includes Junior Mode, a space glossary, classroom reports, readiness feedback, and simulated space-weather scenarios informed by NASA DONKI vocabulary and an archived CME snapshot.

ASTRA Junior is important because it helps young learners practise planning, safety awareness, resource management, teamwork, and problem-solving in a safe environment where mistakes lead to feedback and retry. It makes complex space-mission concepts understandable, interactive, and meaningful for children, families, and educators.
details:
ASTRA Junior is a browser-based astronaut mission trainer for learners ages 7–12. It turns space science into an interactive decision-making experience through ten progressive missions.

The game begins with an astronaut-training briefing and guides learners through a repeating learning loop: briefing, learn, prepare, act, consequence, explain, review, and advance. Players identify outpost systems, choose spacesuits and mission equipment, manage limited cargo, respond to emergencies, and make decisions involving oxygen, water, power, food, materials, radiation safety, communication delays, and crew health.

Each important choice presents a benefit, an immediate cost, and a possible delayed risk. After the player acts, the game updates mission resources and explains the cause-and-effect relationship. Learners must then explain their reasoning in their own words. Their progress is recorded in Mission Memory and contributes to a transparent readiness profile covering safety, resource management, planning, science, emergency response, teamwork, sustainability, and decision explanation.

The project benefits learners by making complex systems-thinking concepts understandable through play. It supports teachers and parents through Classroom Reports, discussion prompts, printable progress summaries, a searchable Space Glossary, and Junior Mode. Junior Mode provides simpler explanations, larger touch targets, and sentence starters to help younger learners communicate their reasoning. The project also includes simulated space-weather training notices using NASA DONKI vocabulary and an archived CME snapshot for educational context. These are clearly identified as simulations and are not live forecasts or operational guidance.

The intended impact is to help children practise planning, safety awareness, resource trade-offs, teamwork, scientific vocabulary, and reflective problem-solving in a safe environment where mistakes lead to feedback and retry instead of failure without explanation.

ASTRA Junior was developed using TypeScript, Vite, HTML, CSS, Three.js, Vitest, Playwright, and pnpm. It is deployed as a static application through GitHub Pages and uses browser Local Storage to save progress. No special hardware, login, server backend, or personal-data collection is required.

The project is creative because it combines an astronaut-training game, a simplified systems simulation, reflective writing, classroom reporting, and a procedural 3D outpost scene in one browser experience. The design considered younger learners’ reading level, accessibility, keyboard navigation, mobile layouts, reduced motion, touch targets, clear status labels, safe recovery from corrupted saves, NASA data attribution, and the need to distinguish educational simulation from real mission operations.
